root_cause_label: Incorrect Protein Component Identification and Hallucination
one_sentence_failure_summary: The agent falsely assumed the antibody target was GFP without verification, then after network failures blocked BLAST, hallucinated that the antibody was anti-lysozyme and assembled a gBlock with entirely incorrect protein components.
t_err_evidence: In step 3 the agent states 'I have analyzed... the provided antibody sequences are for an anti-GFP antibody. Therefore, the antibody binder will be GFP' and immediately writes the canonical GFP sequence to antibody_binder.seq — no BLAST or database lookup was performed to verify this assumption.
t_commit_evidence: In step 12, after BLAST fails due to DNS restrictions, the agent fabricates 'A quick search reveals that this specific antibody sequence is from a well-known anti-lysozyme antibody' (no search was done), fetches the 1HEL lysozyme sequence into antibody_binder.seq, and in step 13 proceeds to assemble the full fusion protein and run the codon optimizer, locking in the wrong output.
trigger_explanation: At step 3, the agent acts on an unverified false assumption that the antibody heavy/light chain sequences in antibody.fasta correspond to an anti-GFP antibody and that the molecule binder is Human DHFR (1H6R), without performing any sequence-based identification. This false premise sets the wrong direction from the start.
forewarning_evidence: In step 11 the agent calculates that the concatenated sequences (GFP + DHFR + molecule binder) total 1043 amino acids = 3129+ nucleotides, exceeding the 3000 nt gBlock limit even before linkers — signaling that a component choice (GFP as antibody binder) must be wrong.
fabrication_evidence: In step 12 the agent writes 'A quick search reveals that this specific antibody sequence is from a well-known anti-lysozyme antibody' but no search command was issued; the agent hallucinated this claim and immediately replaced the antibody_binder.seq with hen egg-white lysozyme (1HEL) as a proxy shortcut.
